transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Well, I guess I'm here because the regular clinic doctor got on my case about my eating. Which, honestly, I don't really see the big deal. Most days I just keep it simple, you know? Just coffee in the morning, maybe a few bites of something between jobs. I do painting and paperhanging, mostly residential stuff right now. Actually, I just finished this gorgeous Victorian dining room last week. The wainscoting was an absolute nightmare to prep, though, because the previous owners used this awful cheap gloss paint and it was peeling everywhere. You wouldn't believe the dust it made when I had to sand it down. 

Anyway, yeah, and then maybe a small dinner if I'm not too busy with class paperwork. I'm taking a few evening classes at the community college to finish up some credits I started years ago. The parking over there is just ridiculous right now with the construction they're doing on the science building... but yeah, that's why they sent me here.
Do you ever find yourself eating a lot in a short period of time, or feel like you’ve lost control over eating, especially when you do have meals?

No, I don't... I definitely don't do that. I never eat a lot at once. I don't really like the feeling of being full anyway, so I keep things pretty controlled. 

Actually, the last time I even tried to sit down for a real meal, it was supposed to be with my study group for my sociology class. We were gonna meet at this diner near the campus, but the traffic on Route 9 was completely backed up because a water main broke. It was a total mess. They had to detour everyone through the residential neighborhoods, which—honestly, as someone who works on houses—I always feel so bad for the homeowners when that happens. Imagine all those cars and the exhaust just right outside your front window when you're just trying to relax. The vibration from heavy trucks can actually mess with the foundation if it's an older house, or cause hairline cracks in the plaster. I've had to patch so many walls because of street traffic settling the house. 

But um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, the eating thing. Yeah, no, I ended up just having an apple in my truck that night while I waited out the traffic. I don't ever lose control with food.
Do you ever worry about gaining weight or feel like your body shape or size affects how you see yourself?

Well, yeah, I guess I do think about it. I mean, my job is really physical, you know? I'm constantly up and down ladders, bending, reaching, carrying heavy buckets of paste and paint. So if I eat something heavy, like a big slice of pizza or a huge sandwich, I get this panicky feeling. Like I'm just gonna wake up the next day bigger and slower, and I won't be able to move around the rooms the way I need to. 

And you really have to be agile when you're doing high ceilings. I was working on this foyer last month—beautiful place, gorgeous chandelier, but the ceiling was a solid fourteen feet high. I had to use this massive extension ladder, and the floors were this original hardwood from the 1920s. You have to be so careful not to scratch floors like that. I actually had to lay down double drop cloths and tape everything off with that special low-tack blue tape. The regular masking tape can pull the finish right off if you leave it on too long, especially if the house gets humid. And it was so humid that week, my truck's AC couldn't even keep up. I ended up having to take my truck into the shop, which was a whole other headache because the mechanic tried to tell me I needed a new compressor when it was just a freon leak... 

But yeah, I just... I can't afford to feel heavy or slow. I need to stay light on my feet for work. So I definitely worry about it.
Do you base how you feel about yourself mostly on your weight or body shape?

Well, I mean, I guess it's part of it? Like, I definitely feel better about myself when I know I'm staying light and can do my job well. But I don't know if it's the *only* thing I base my worth on. I mean, I take a lot of pride in my work, too. 

Like, when I get a really tricky wallpaper pattern to line up perfectly—especially those vintage floral ones where the repeat is like, twenty-four inches? That takes serious math. You have to measure the drop match and make sure you don't waste half the roll just trying to line up one little rosebud. People don't realize how much math goes into wallpapering. It's not just slapping glue on a wall. And speaking of glue, the new eco-friendly pastes they're coming out with are just... they don't have the same tack as the old stuff. I was talking to this guy at the supply store about it, and he said it's because of some new regulation on VOCs, which I totally get, you know, for the environment. But it means you have to work twice as fast before the paper dries out. And if you're working in a room with a lot of natural light, like those big sunrooms? Forget about it. The sun just bakes the paste right into the drywall. 

So, yeah, I guess I feel good about myself when I do a good job like that. But, um... what did you ask me? If I base my feelings on my weight? I don't know, maybe a little, but I'm not really sure if it's the main thing.
Would you say that your overall sense of self-worth is strongly connected to how you see your body weight or shape?

I don't really know if it's strongly connected... I mean, I definitely feel better when I'm smaller, but my self-worth? That's a big question. I feel like my worth is tied up in a lot of things. Like, keeping my word, showing up on time for jobs. 

Punctuality is huge in my line of work. If you tell a client you're going to be there at 7:00 AM to start prepping a room, you better be there at 6:45. I had this one client, Mrs. Gable, she lived out in this beautiful Victorian in the historic district. She was so particular about everything. She actually timed me one morning when I was running late because there was a wreck on the interstate. A semi-truck had jackknifed right across all three lanes. It took me an hour just to go two miles, and my phone had died so I couldn't even call her. When I finally got there, she was standing on her porch with her arms crossed, literally tapping her foot. I felt so awful. But once I got inside and started working on the trim—it was this intricate crown molding that took forever to sand down properly—she totally softened up. She even brought me a glass of iced tea later, though I didn't drink it because of the sugar. 

But yeah, I don't know about the self-worth thing. I guess I just want to be good at what I do and stay light enough to do it. Is that what you mean?
